pairs.pattern: WHAT IS SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT
pairs.response: Software development is the path from an agreement about the work to software people can use, and that someone else can maintain. You learn what the system must do, design it, build it, test it, and write down what you learned along the way. The steps can overlap and repeat. Nothing here requires you to finish one step for the whole system before the next step starts.

pairs.pattern: WHAT IS MIL STD 498
pairs.response: MIL-STD-498 is a 1994 checklist for that path. It was written for defense projects, and the useful part is ordinary: which work to do, and which information to write down. It does not choose a programming language or insist on a waterfall. The documents are collected at https://github.com/VCTLabs/MIL-STD-498.

pairs.pattern: WHAT ARE THE SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITIES
pairs.response: Start by planning the work and setting up the tools. Then learn how people will use the system, what the whole system must do, and what the software itself must do. Design the system, then the software. Build it and test the pieces, then the pieces together, then the software against its own requirements, then the software with the hardware, then the whole system. After that, prepare it for the people who will use it, and for the people who will maintain it. The whole time, keep versions under control, check the work, track problems, and review progress with the customer.

pairs.pattern: DOES SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT HAVE TO BE A WATERFALL
pairs.response: No. The steps may overlap, repeat, and apply differently to different parts of the software. You describe the way you will actually work, including whether you will deliver in a series of builds. A build is one version that does a stated part of the job.

pairs.pattern: WHAT IS A SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT PLAN
pairs.response: The software development plan is where you say how this project will actually run. Name the builds, the steps you will perform, the methods and tools, the standards for requirements, design, code, and tests, the schedule, and who does the work. The customer agrees to that plan. When it changes, they agree again, except for the team's internal schedule and staffing.

pairs.pattern: WHAT PLANS DOES A SOFTWARE PROJECT NEED
pairs.response: Four plans usually matter. How you will develop the software. How you will test it against its requirements. How you will install it. How you will hand it to the people who will maintain it. The customer approves those plans. Write a plan only for the work this project really has.

pairs.pattern: WHAT IS A SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT LIBRARY
pairs.response: The library is the controlled collection of the software and the information that belongs with it. A development file is the working record for one piece: what it is for, how it was built, and how it was tested. The library is the shelf. The file is the notes on one thing on that shelf.

pairs.pattern: SHOULD I WRITE THINGS DOWN OR DELIVER A DOCUMENT
pairs.response: Writing the information down is part of the work. Handing the customer a formal copy is a separate choice. The notes can be a document, a file, or what already lives in a design tool. The checklist is the same either way: someone later has to be able to find what was decided.

pairs.pattern: WHO IS THE CUSTOMER IN A SOFTWARE PROJECT
pairs.response: The customer is who asked for the software and agrees the plans. The team is who builds it. Users are the people who will use the results. Maintainers are the people who will look after it once development is done, when that is a different group. Those can be four different groups, or some of them can be the same people. Say which is which.

pairs.pattern: WHAT IS A REVIEW WITH THE CUSTOMER
pairs.response: Hold two kinds of review with the customer. A technical review looks at the work itself, such as the requirements or the design. A management review looks at progress, risks, and whether the plan still fits. The development plan says which reviews you will actually hold.

pairs.pattern: WHAT IS VERSION CONTROL IN A PROJECT
pairs.response: Name the things you will version. Decide who may change each one, and what a change has to go through. Keep a record of what was proposed and what was done. Check that the software you ship matches what you documented and tested. Then pack and deliver that same version, not a later one that slipped in.

pairs.pattern: HOW DO I HANDLE A PROBLEM IN THE SOFTWARE
pairs.response: Write the problem down: who found it, what it affects, how serious it is, and what you decided to do. Track it until a specific version contains the fix, and check that the fix worked. The same loop covers a requested change, not only a defect.

pairs.pattern: WHAT IF ANOTHER TEAM IS BUILDING PART OF THIS
